doc.title: Melba Liston — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Annie's Dance and Dizzy's diplomacy
summary: Annie's Dance broke the ice abroad, Liston says she was not playing politics, and credits Dizzy for keeping the band together.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: But it’s been said over there, at the State Department – on a State Department tour, that your arrangement on My Reverie – no, Anitra’s Dance – Annie’s Dance would break the ice, because there was – they recognized the theme and they liked your arrangement – treatment of it. Is that true?
Dizzy and you had to play politics?
I don’t know if – I was just doing whatever . . .
. . . and he was just doing whatever. We weren’t no – I wasn’t doing any politics.
I know. I know you weren’t.
Dizzy, I guess, was doing it, but we didn’t see it. I didn’t know that Dizzy was doing everything that he was doing to keep us together and all that.
